paragraphs: Towards the end of the last century, there lived a distinguished scientist who was highly skilled in every branch of natural philosophy. Shortly before our story begins, he had discovered a spiritual attraction stronger than any chemical one. He left his laboratory in an assistant’s care, cleared the furnace smoke from his handsome face, washed the acid stains from his fingers, and persuaded a beautiful woman to become his wife. In those days, the relatively recent discovery of electricity and other mysteries of Nature seemed to open paths into the realm of miracles. It was not unusual for the love of science to rival the love of a woman in depth and absorbing intensity. The higher intellect, imagination, spirit and even the heart could all find satisfying nourishment in scientific pursuits. Some passionate followers believed these pursuits would climb from one level of powerful understanding to another, until the philosopher grasped the secret of creation itself and perhaps made new worlds of his own. We do not know whether Aylmer had such faith in humanity’s eventual control over Nature. But he had devoted himself too completely to scientific study ever to be drawn away from it by a second passion. His love for his young wife might prove the stronger of the two. It could do so, however, only by intertwining with his love of science and joining that love’s strength to its own.

Such a union did take place, with truly remarkable consequences and a deeply impressive moral. One day, very soon after their marriage, Aylmer sat gazing at his wife. The troubled expression on his face grew stronger until he spoke.
‘Georgiana,’ he said, ‘have you never thought that the mark on your cheek might be removed?’

‘No, indeed,’ she said, smiling. But when she saw how serious he was, she blushed deeply. ‘To tell you the truth, people have so often called it a charm that I was simple enough to think it might be one.’

‘Ah, perhaps it might be on another face,’ her husband replied, ‘but never on yours. No, dearest Georgiana, you came so nearly perfect from Nature’s hand that this smallest possible flaw shocks me. We can scarcely decide whether to call it a flaw or a beauty, yet to me it is the visible mark of earthly imperfection.’

‘Shocks you, my husband!’ Georgiana cried, deeply hurt. She flushed with a moment’s anger, then burst into tears. ‘Then why did you take me away from my mother’s side? You cannot love what shocks you!’

To explain this conversation, I must mention a peculiar mark in the centre of Georgiana’s left cheek. It seemed woven deeply into the texture and substance of her face. Her usual complexion had a healthy but delicate bloom. Against it, the mark was a deeper crimson, its shape only partly distinct amid the surrounding rosiness. When she blushed, it gradually became less visible, until it disappeared in the triumphant rush of blood that bathed her whole cheek in a brilliant glow. But if a change made her turn pale, the mark reappeared: a crimson stain on snow, so distinct that Aylmer sometimes found it almost frightening. Its shape closely resembled a human hand, though on the tiniest possible scale. Georgiana’s admirers used to say that at the hour of her birth, a fairy had laid her little hand on the baby’s cheek. She had left the imprint as a sign of the magical gifts that would give Georgiana such power over every heart. Many a desperate suitor would have risked his life for the privilege of pressing his lips to that mysterious hand. Yet it must be admitted that this fairy signature affected people very differently, according to their temperaments. Some fastidious people—all of them women—declared that the bloody hand, as they chose to call it, completely spoiled Georgiana’s beauty and even made her face hideous. But one might as reasonably say that one of the small blue stains sometimes found in the purest sculptural marble would turn Powers’s Eve into a monster. Male observers, if the birthmark did not increase their admiration, contented themselves with wishing it away. Then the world might possess one living example of ideal beauty without the appearance of a flaw. After his marriage, Aylmer discovered that he felt this way himself. Beforehand, he had given the matter little or no thought.

Had she been less beautiful—had Envy herself found anything else to sneer at—he might have loved her all the more for the prettiness of this little imitation hand. Sometimes its outline was faint, sometimes it disappeared, and sometimes it crept out again, glimmering to and fro with every pulse of emotion in her heart. But because she was otherwise so perfect, he found this single flaw more intolerable with every moment of their married life. It was humanity’s fatal flaw, which Nature stamps indelibly, in one form or another, on everything she creates. Perhaps it means that her creations are temporary and limited, or that their perfection must be achieved through toil and pain. The crimson hand expressed the inescapable grip with which mortality seizes the highest and purest earthly beings. It lowers them into kinship with the lowest, even with animals, whose visible bodies, like theirs, return to dust. Aylmer chose the mark as a symbol of his wife’s vulnerability to sin, sorrow, decay and death. His sombre imagination soon made it an object of terror, bringing him more distress and horror than Georgiana’s beauty, whether of soul or body, had ever given him delight.

At the times when they should have been happiest, he always returned to this disastrous subject. He did so unintentionally, indeed despite his intention not to. Trivial as it had first seemed, it became linked to so many trains of thought and ways of feeling that it became the centre of them all. In the morning twilight, Aylmer opened his eyes on his wife’s face and recognised the symbol of imperfection. When they sat together by the evening hearth, his eyes stole towards her cheek. There, flickering in the wood fire’s blaze, he saw the ghostly hand that wrote mortality where he would gladly have worshipped. Georgiana soon learned to shudder at his gaze. One glance with that particular expression he so often wore was enough to turn her rosy cheek deathly pale. Against that pallor, the crimson hand stood out sharply, like a ruby relief carving on the whitest marble.
Late one night, when the lights had grown so dim that they barely revealed the stain on the poor wife’s cheek, she brought up the subject herself for the first time.
‘Do you remember, my dear Aylmer,’ she said, trying weakly to smile, ‘do you remember a dream last night about this hateful hand?’

‘No! Not at all!’ Aylmer replied with a start. Then, in a dry, cold tone adopted to hide the real depth of his emotion, he added, ‘I might well dream of it. Before I fell asleep, it had taken a fairly firm hold on my imagination.’

‘And you did dream of it?’ Georgiana continued quickly, afraid that a flood of tears would interrupt what she had to say. ‘A terrible dream! I wonder how you can forget it. Can you possibly forget these words: “It is in her heart now; we must have it out!” Think, my husband. I want you, by every means, to remember that dream.’

The mind is in a sad state when all-enveloping Sleep cannot keep her ghosts within the dim region she rules. Instead, she lets them break out and frighten our waking lives with secrets that may belong to a deeper life. Aylmer now remembered his dream. He had imagined himself and his servant Aminadab attempting an operation to remove the birthmark. But the deeper the knife went, the deeper the hand sank. At last its tiny grip seemed to have seized Georgiana’s heart. Even then, her husband was unshakably determined to cut or wrench it away.

When the dream had taken complete shape in his memory, Aylmer sat before his wife feeling guilty. Truth often reaches the mind closely wrapped in the robes of sleep. It then speaks with uncompromising directness about matters on which we unknowingly deceive ourselves while awake. Until now, he had not realised how tyrannically this one idea ruled his mind, or how far he might find it in his heart to go in order to give himself peace.

‘Aylmer,’ Georgiana continued solemnly, ‘I do not know what it may cost us both to rid me of this fatal birthmark. Removing it may cause a deformity that can never be cured. Or perhaps the stain goes as deep as life itself. And do we know whether, at any price, it is possible to loosen the firm grip of this little hand, laid on me before I came into the world?’
‘Dearest Georgiana, I have thought deeply about this,’ Aylmer interrupted quickly. ‘I am convinced that removing it is entirely possible.’

‘If there is the slightest possibility,’ Georgiana continued, ‘let us make the attempt, whatever the risk. Danger means nothing to me. Life—while this hateful mark makes me an object of horror and disgust to you—life is a burden I would gladly throw down. Either remove this dreadful hand or take my miserable life! Your scientific knowledge is profound. The whole world testifies to it. You have achieved great wonders. Can you not remove this little, little mark, which I can cover with the tips of two small fingers? Is that beyond your power, for the sake of your own peace and to save your poor wife from madness?’

‘My noblest, dearest, tenderest wife!’ Aylmer cried in rapture. ‘Do not doubt my power. I have already given this the deepest thought—thought that might almost have taught me to create a being less perfect than you. Georgiana, you have led me farther than ever into the heart of science. I feel entirely capable of making this dear cheek as faultless as the other. And then, my most beloved, what a triumph it will be to have corrected what Nature left imperfect in her fairest creation! Even Pygmalion, when his sculptured woman came to life, felt no greater ecstasy than I shall.’
‘Then it is decided,’ Georgiana said with a faint smile. ‘And, Aylmer, do not spare me, even if you find that the birthmark has finally taken refuge in my heart.’
Her husband tenderly kissed her cheek—her right cheek, not the one marked with the crimson hand.

The next day, Aylmer told his wife about a plan he had devised. It would give him the opportunity for the intense thought and constant watchfulness the proposed operation required, while allowing Georgiana the complete rest essential to its success. They would shut themselves away in the extensive rooms Aylmer used as a laboratory. There, during his hardworking youth, he had made discoveries about Nature’s elemental powers that had won the admiration of all Europe’s learned societies. Sitting calmly in this laboratory, the pale philosopher had investigated the secrets of the highest cloud regions and the deepest mines. He had satisfied himself about what ignited volcanoes and kept their fires burning. He had explained the mystery of springs: why they gush from the earth’s dark breast, some so bright and pure, others so rich in medicinal properties. Earlier still, he had studied the wonders of the human body. He had tried to understand the very process by which Nature draws together all her precious influences from earth, air and the spiritual world to create and nurture humanity, her masterpiece. Aylmer had long since abandoned that last pursuit. Reluctantly, he had recognised a truth against which all investigators sooner or later stumble. Our great creative Mother amuses us by appearing to work in the broadest sunshine, yet jealously guards her secrets. Despite her pretended openness, she shows us only results. She allows us to spoil things, but seldom to mend them, and, like a jealous patent holder, never to create them. Now Aylmer took up those half-forgotten investigations again. Of course, he no longer had the hopes and wishes that first inspired them. He returned to them because they involved many truths about the body’s workings and lay along the route of his proposed treatment for Georgiana.

As he led her across the laboratory’s threshold, Georgiana was cold and trembling. Aylmer looked cheerfully into her face to reassure her. But the birthmark glowed so intensely against her white cheek that he was startled into a violent, convulsive shudder he could not suppress. His wife fainted.
‘Aminadab! Aminadab!’ Aylmer shouted, stamping violently on the floor.

A short, bulky man immediately emerged from an inner room. Shaggy hair hung about his face, which was grimy with furnace fumes. He had been Aylmer’s assistant throughout his scientific career. His great mechanical dexterity made him admirably suited to the work. Though he could not understand a single principle, he skilfully carried out every detail of his master’s experiments. With his immense strength, shaggy hair, smoky appearance and the indescribable earthiness that seemed to crust him over, he appeared to represent humanity’s physical nature. Aylmer’s slender figure and pale, intellectual face represented the spiritual element just as aptly.
‘Throw open the door of the private sitting room, Aminadab,’ Aylmer said, ‘and burn a scented tablet.’
‘Yes, master,’ Aminadab answered, looking intently at Georgiana’s lifeless form. Then he muttered to himself, ‘If she were my wife, I would never part with that birthmark.’

When Georgiana regained consciousness, she found herself breathing air filled with a penetrating fragrance. Its gentle power had brought her out of her deathlike faint. The scene around her looked enchanted. Aylmer had transformed those smoky, dingy, gloomy rooms, where he had spent his brightest years on obscure investigations, into a series of beautiful apartments fit to be a lovely woman’s secluded home. Gorgeous curtains covered the walls, combining grandeur with grace as no other decoration can. Falling from ceiling to floor, their rich, heavy folds hid every angle and straight line, seeming to shut off the scene from infinite space. For all Georgiana knew, it might have been a pavilion among the clouds. Aylmer had shut out the sunshine because it would interfere with his chemical processes. In its place he provided perfumed lamps, whose differently coloured flames blended into a soft, purplish radiance. He now knelt beside his wife, watching her intently but without alarm. He trusted his science and felt that he could draw a magic circle around her into which no evil could enter.
‘Where am I? Ah, I remember,’ Georgiana said faintly. She covered her cheek with her hand to hide the terrible mark from her husband’s eyes.
‘Do not be afraid, dearest!’ he exclaimed. ‘Do not shrink from me! Believe me, Georgiana, I even rejoice in this one imperfection, because removing it will bring such rapture.’
‘Oh, spare me!’ his wife replied sadly. ‘Please do not look at it again. I can never forget that convulsive shudder.’

To soothe Georgiana and free her mind, as it were, from the burden of real things, Aylmer now used some of the light, playful secrets science had taught him alongside its deeper knowledge. Airy figures, ideas without any physical body, and forms of insubstantial beauty appeared and danced before her, leaving their momentary footprints on beams of light. She had some vague understanding of how these optical effects were produced. Even so, the illusion was almost perfect enough to justify a belief that her husband ruled the spiritual world. Then, when she wished to look beyond her seclusion, the passing procession of life outside immediately flitted across a screen, as if in answer to her thoughts. The scenery and figures of real life appeared perfectly reproduced. Yet they had that enchanting, indescribable difference that always makes a picture, image or shadow so much more attractive than its original. When she tired of this, Aylmer asked her to look at a container holding some soil. She did so, at first with little interest. Soon, however, she was startled to see a plant’s first shoot rising from the earth. A slender stalk followed, the leaves gradually unfolded, and among them appeared a perfect, lovely flower.
‘It’s magical!’ Georgiana cried. ‘I dare not touch it.’

‘No, pick it,’ Aylmer answered. ‘Pick it and breathe its short-lived fragrance while you can. In a few moments the flower will wither, leaving only its brown seed cases. But from those, a succession of plants as short-lived as this one may be continued.’
But the moment Georgiana touched the flower, the whole plant was blighted. Its leaves turned coal-black, as though burned by fire.
‘The stimulus was too powerful,’ Aylmer said thoughtfully.

To make up for this failed experiment, he offered to make her portrait by a scientific process he had invented. Rays of light would strike a polished metal plate to produce it. Georgiana agreed. But when she looked at the result, she was frightened to find the portrait’s features blurred and indistinct, while a tiny image of a hand appeared where the cheek should have been. Aylmer snatched the metal plate and threw it into a jar of corrosive acid.

Soon, however, he forgot these humiliating failures. Between periods of study and chemical experiment, he came to her flushed and exhausted. Her presence seemed to revive him, and he spoke in glowing terms of the resources of his art. He described the long line of alchemists who had spent so many ages searching for a universal solvent, by which the principle of gold might be drawn from everything vile and base. Aylmer seemed to believe that the simplest scientific reasoning showed it was entirely possible to discover this long-sought substance. ‘But,’ he added, ‘a philosopher who went deep enough to gain that power would reach a wisdom too lofty to stoop to using it.’ His opinions about the elixir of life were no less strange. He more than hinted that, if he chose, he could prepare a liquid that would prolong life for years, perhaps for ever. But it would introduce a discord into Nature that the whole world, and especially whoever drank the potion for immortality, would have reason to curse.
‘Aylmer, are you serious?’ Georgiana asked, looking at him in amazement and fear. ‘It is terrible to have such power, or even to dream of having it.’

‘Oh, do not tremble, my love,’ her husband said. ‘I would not wrong you or myself by bringing such disharmony into our lives. But consider how little skill, by comparison, is needed to remove this little hand.’
At the mention of the birthmark, Georgiana shrank as usual, as though a red-hot iron had touched her cheek.

Aylmer returned to his work. She could hear him in the distant furnace room giving instructions to Aminadab. His assistant’s harsh, rough, misshapen voice answered, sounding more like an animal’s grunt or growl than human speech. After several hours away, Aylmer returned and suggested that she examine his cabinet of chemical preparations and natural treasures from the earth. Among the preparations, he showed her a small vial. It contained, he said, a gentle but immensely powerful fragrance, capable of scenting every breeze that blew across a kingdom. The contents of that little vial were beyond price. As he said so, he scattered some of the perfume into the air, filling the room with a penetrating, invigorating delight.
‘And what is this?’ Georgiana asked, pointing to a little crystal globe containing a golden liquid. ‘It looks so beautiful that I could imagine it was the elixir of life.’

‘In one sense it is,’ Aylmer replied, ‘or rather, the elixir of immortality. It is the most precious poison ever made in this world. With it, I could determine the lifespan of any mortal you chose to point out. The strength of the dose would decide whether he lingered for years or dropped dead in the middle of a breath. No king on his guarded throne could keep his life if I, a private citizen, decided that the welfare of millions justified my taking it.’
‘Why do you keep such a terrifying drug?’ Georgiana asked in horror.

‘Do not distrust me, dearest,’ her husband said with a smile. ‘Its power to do good is even greater than its power to harm. But look! Here is a powerful cosmetic. A few drops in a vase of water will wash away freckles as easily as you wash your hands. A stronger mixture would drain the blood from the cheek and turn the rosiest beauty into a pale ghost.’
‘Is that the lotion you intend to bathe my cheek with?’ Georgiana asked anxiously.
‘Oh, no,’ her husband replied quickly. ‘This works only on the surface. Your case needs a remedy that goes deeper.’

When Aylmer spoke with Georgiana, he usually questioned her closely about her sensations and whether the confinement of the rooms and the temperature of the air suited her. His questions took such a particular direction that she began to suspect she was already being exposed to certain physical influences, either breathed in with the fragrant air or taken in her food. She also imagined—but it might have been entirely imagination—that something was stirring within her body. A strange, indefinite sensation crept through her veins and tingled at her heart, half painful and half pleasurable. Yet whenever she dared to look in the mirror, she saw herself pale as a white rose, with the crimson birthmark stamped on her cheek. Not even Aylmer hated it as much as she now did.

To relieve the boredom of the hours her husband had to spend combining and analysing substances, Georgiana browsed through his scientific library. In many dark old volumes she found chapters full of romance and poetry. They were works by medieval philosophers such as Albertus Magnus, Cornelius Agrippa, Paracelsus, and the famous friar who created the prophetic Brazen Head. These early students of Nature were ahead of their centuries, yet shared some of their credulity. People therefore believed, and perhaps the men themselves imagined, that studying Nature had given them power above Nature, and that physics had given them command over the spiritual world. The early volumes of the Transactions of the Royal Society were almost as strange and imaginative. Knowing little about the limits of natural possibility, its members constantly recorded wonders or proposed methods for producing them.

But the book that absorbed Georgiana most was a large folio in her husband’s own handwriting. He had recorded every experiment of his scientific career: its original purpose, the methods used to develop it, its final success or failure, and the circumstances responsible for either result. The book was both the history and the emblem of his passionate, ambitious, imaginative, yet practical and hardworking life. He dealt with physical details as if nothing existed beyond them. Yet he gave them all a spiritual character, redeeming himself from materialism through his strong, eager longing for the infinite. In his grasp, the merest clod of earth took on a soul. As Georgiana read, she revered Aylmer and loved him more deeply than ever, but depended less completely on his judgement than before. Despite all he had achieved, she could not help seeing that his most splendid successes were almost always failures beside the ideal he aimed at. His brightest diamonds were mere pebbles—and he felt them to be so—compared with the priceless gems hidden beyond his reach. Though rich in achievements that had brought its author fame, the volume was as melancholy a record as any mortal hand had written. It was a sad confession, and a continual demonstration, of the failings of humanity’s mixed nature: spirit burdened with clay and working in matter. It showed the despair that attacks the higher nature when it finds itself so miserably thwarted by the earthly part. Perhaps every person of genius, in any field, could recognise an image of their own experience in Aylmer’s journal.
These reflections affected Georgiana so deeply that she laid her face on the open book and burst into tears. Her husband found her like this.

‘It is dangerous to read a sorcerer’s books,’ he said with a smile, though his face was uneasy and displeased. ‘Georgiana, there are pages in that book I can scarcely glance at and keep my senses. Be careful that it does not harm you in the same way.’
‘It has made me worship you more than ever,’ she said.

‘Ah, wait for this one success,’ he replied, ‘then worship me if you wish. I shall hardly consider myself unworthy of it. But come, I sought you out for the luxury of your voice. Sing to me, dearest.’

So she poured out her voice’s liquid music to quench his spirit’s thirst. Afterwards he left her with a boy’s exuberant happiness. He assured her that her seclusion would last only a little longer and that the result was already certain. He had scarcely gone when Georgiana felt an irresistible urge to follow him. She had forgotten to tell Aylmer about a symptom that had begun to attract her attention over the last two or three hours. It was a sensation in the fatal birthmark, painless but making her restless throughout her body. Hurrying after her husband, she intruded into the laboratory for the first time.

The first thing she noticed was the furnace, that hot, feverish worker, with its intensely glowing fire. The soot clustered above it suggested that it had been burning for ages. Distilling equipment was in full operation. Around the room stood distilling flasks, tubes, cylinders, crucibles and other apparatus for chemical research. An electrical machine was ready for immediate use. The air was oppressively close, tainted with gaseous smells forced out by the torments of scientific processes. After the fantastic elegance of her private sitting room, the laboratory’s severe, plain simplicity, with its bare walls and brick floor, looked strange to Georgiana. But what drew her attention most, indeed almost exclusively, was Aylmer’s own appearance.

He was deathly pale, anxious and absorbed. He bent over the furnace as though his utmost vigilance would decide whether the liquid being distilled there became a drink of immortal happiness or misery. How different he looked from the hopeful, joyful manner he had adopted to encourage Georgiana!

‘Carefully now, Aminadab; carefully, you human machine; carefully, you man of clay!’ Aylmer muttered, more to himself than to his assistant. ‘Now, if there is the slightest bit too much or too little, it is all over.’
‘Ho! Ho!’ Aminadab mumbled. ‘Look, master! Look!’
Aylmer quickly looked up. At the sight of Georgiana, he first reddened, then turned paler than ever. He rushed towards her and gripped her arm so tightly that his fingers left marks on it.
‘Why have you come here? Do you have no trust in your husband?’ he cried fiercely. ‘Would you cast the blight of that fatal birthmark over my work? This is wrong of you. Go, prying woman, go!’

‘No, Aylmer,’ Georgiana said with a firmness she possessed in no small measure. ‘You are not the one with a right to complain. You distrust your wife. You have hidden the anxiety with which you watch this experiment develop. Do not think so poorly of me, my husband. Tell me every risk we face, and do not fear that I will shrink from it. My share in it is far less than yours.’
‘No, no, Georgiana!’ Aylmer said impatiently. ‘It must not be.’
‘I submit,’ she replied calmly. ‘And, Aylmer, I shall drink whatever you bring me. But I shall do so for the same reason that I would take a dose of poison if your hand offered it.’

‘My noble wife,’ Aylmer said, deeply moved, ‘until now I did not know the height and depth of your nature. I shall hide nothing. Know, then, that this crimson hand, though it seems to lie only on the surface, has gripped your very being with a strength I never imagined. I have already given you substances powerful enough to do anything except change your entire physical system. Only one thing remains to be tried. If it fails us, we are ruined.’
‘Why did you hesitate to tell me this?’ she asked.
‘Because, Georgiana,’ Aylmer said softly, ‘there is danger.’
‘Danger? There is only one danger—that this horrible mark of disgrace will remain on my cheek!’ Georgiana cried. ‘Remove it, remove it, whatever the cost, or we shall both go mad!’
‘Heaven knows your words are all too true,’ Aylmer said sadly. ‘And now, dearest, return to your private sitting room. In a little while, everything will be put to the test.’

He took her back and left her with a solemn tenderness that showed far more clearly than words how much was now at stake. After he left, Georgiana became absorbed in reflection. She considered Aylmer’s character and did it fuller justice than ever before. Her heart rejoiced, even as it trembled, at his honourable love. It was so pure and lofty that it would accept nothing less than perfection. It would not miserably settle for a nature more earthly than the one he had dreamed of. She felt how much more precious this was than a lesser love that would have tolerated the flaw for her sake. Such a love would have betrayed holy love by lowering its perfect ideal to the level of reality. With her whole spirit, she prayed that she might satisfy his highest and deepest conception for a single moment. She knew very well that it could not last longer. His spirit was always marching onwards, always ascending, and each instant demanded something beyond the reach of the one before.

Her husband’s footsteps roused her. He carried a crystal goblet containing a liquid as colourless as water, but bright enough to be a drink of immortality. Aylmer was pale, though this seemed to come from an intensely excited mind and a tension of spirit rather than fear or doubt.
‘The drink has been prepared perfectly,’ he said in answer to Georgiana’s look. ‘Unless all my science has deceived me, it cannot fail.’

‘Except for your sake, my dearest Aylmer,’ his wife observed, ‘I might prefer to cast off this birthmark of mortality by giving up mortal life itself, rather than in any other way. Life is only a sad possession for those who have reached precisely the stage of moral development where I stand. If I were weaker and blinder, it might be happiness. If I were stronger, I might endure it with hope. But being what I am, I think I am the most fit to die of all mortals.’
‘You are fit for heaven without tasting death!’ her husband replied. ‘But why are we speaking of dying? The drink cannot fail. Look at its effect on this plant.’

On the window seat stood a geranium, diseased with yellow blotches that covered all its leaves. Aylmer poured a little of the liquid onto the soil it grew in. Soon, when the roots had absorbed the moisture, the ugly blotches began to disappear into a living greenness.
‘No proof was needed,’ Georgiana said quietly. ‘Give me the goblet. I gladly stake everything on your word.’
‘Then drink, you exalted creature!’ Aylmer exclaimed with passionate admiration. ‘There is no stain of imperfection on your spirit. Your physical body, too, will soon be entirely perfect.’
She drank the liquid and handed the goblet back to him.

‘It is pleasant,’ she said with a peaceful smile. ‘It seems like water from a heavenly spring, with some subtle fragrance and deliciousness I cannot describe. It eases a feverish thirst that has parched me for many days. Now, dearest, let me sleep. My earthly senses are closing over my spirit like leaves around the heart of a rose at sunset.’

She spoke the last words with gentle reluctance, as though pronouncing those faint, lingering syllables required almost more energy than she could summon. They had scarcely drifted through her lips before she was lost in sleep. Aylmer sat beside her, watching her with the feelings of a man whose life’s entire value was bound up in the process now being tested. Yet mixed with these feelings was the investigative curiosity characteristic of a scientist. Not the smallest symptom escaped him. A deeper flush in her cheek, a slight irregularity of breath, a quivering eyelid, a barely visible tremor through her body: as the moments passed, he wrote these details in his folio. Intense thought had stamped every earlier page of that book, but years of thought were concentrated on the last.

As he worked, he often looked at the fatal hand, shuddering as he did so. Yet once, moved by a strange, inexplicable impulse, he pressed his lips to it. Even as he did so, his spirit recoiled. Deep in her sleep, Georgiana stirred uneasily and murmured as though protesting. Aylmer resumed his watch, and it was not in vain. The crimson hand had at first stood out sharply against the marble pallor of Georgiana’s cheek. Now its outline grew fainter. She remained as pale as ever, but with every breath she took, the birthmark lost some of its former distinctness. Its presence had been terrible; its departure was more terrible still. Watch the colour of a rainbow fade from the sky, and you will know how that mysterious symbol passed away.

‘By Heaven, it is almost gone!’ Aylmer said to himself, scarcely able to contain his ecstasy. ‘I can barely trace it now. Success! Success! Now it is the faintest rose colour. The slightest flush of blood across her cheek would overcome it. But she is so pale!’

He pulled aside the window curtain and let natural daylight enter the room and fall on her cheek. At the same time, he heard a coarse, hoarse chuckle, which he had long recognised as his servant Aminadab’s expression of delight.

‘Ah, clod! Ah, lump of earth!’ Aylmer cried, laughing in a kind of frenzy. ‘You have served me well! Matter and spirit—earth and heaven—have both done their part in this! Laugh, creature of the senses! You have earned the right to laugh.’

His exclamations woke Georgiana. She slowly opened her eyes and looked into the mirror her husband had arranged for her. A faint smile passed over her lips when she saw how barely visible the crimson hand had become. Once it had blazed with such disastrous brilliance that it frightened away all their happiness. But then she looked towards Aylmer’s face with a distress and anxiety he could not explain.
‘My poor Aylmer!’ she murmured.
‘Poor? No—the richest, happiest, most favoured!’ he exclaimed. ‘My peerless bride, it has succeeded! You are perfect!’

‘My poor Aylmer,’ she repeated with a tenderness beyond the human, ‘you have aimed high and acted nobly. Do not regret that, with feelings so lofty and pure, you have rejected the best the earth could offer. Aylmer, dearest Aylmer, I am dying!’

Alas, it was all too true! The fatal hand had gripped the mystery of life itself. It was the bond that kept an angelic spirit united with a mortal body. As the birthmark’s last crimson tint—that sole sign of human imperfection—faded from her cheek, the now perfect woman’s final breath passed into the air. Her soul lingered a moment near her husband, then flew towards heaven. Again, a hoarse, chuckling laugh was heard! So earth’s coarse, fatal power always rejoices in its unfailing triumph over the immortal essence. Here, in this dim sphere of partial development, that essence demands the completeness of a higher state. Yet if Alymer had reached a deeper wisdom, he need not have thrown away a happiness that would have woven his mortal life from the very same fabric as the heavenly. The circumstances of the moment were too strong for him. He failed to look beyond the shadowy limits of time and, by living once and for all in eternity, find the perfect future in the present.
